title: AC Repair Meyerland, Houston | AC Repair Houston
description: Houses from the 1920s to the 1950s in a designated historic district, where exterior equipment changes need review and the ground floods.
intro: Meyerland has rules that most Houston neighborhoods do not. Because the area is a designated historic district, the visible parts of the exterior, including where mechanical equipment goes and how it is screened, go through a review before the work starts. The houses themselves are from the 1920s through the 1950s, and much of the ground near Brays Bayou floods, which is why so many of them sit on raised foundations with the mechanical equipment below the living floor.
localAngle: These are masonry houses from the 1920s, 30s and 50s, and the canopy over the streets is one of the densest in the city, with mature oaks and elms dropping leaf litter onto everything below. Where the ground is low, the house was built up on piers or a raised foundation with a crawlspace underneath, so the air handler, duct trunk and condensate line live in a damp space under the floor. The bayou floods on heavy rain, and that flood puts water in this space. Historic review adds a second constraint: the unit may not go wherever is convenient.
commonCalls: Crawlspace air handlers that have been standing in water after the bayou backs up
Condensate lines that drain into a yard where the grade does not fall away from the house
Outdoor units that need to be screened or relocated to meet historic district rules
Systems that were repaired year after year and now need a refrigerant that is no longer made
Raised foundations where the duct run was left hanging below the joists and now sags

faqs.q: Do I need approval to put a new outdoor unit on my property?
faqs.a: In a designated historic district, visible changes to the exterior of a property generally go through a review before they are made, and a new condenser, a new pad or a screening wall can all fall under it. The district does not review the cooling equipment itself. What it reviews is what you can see from the street. Getting that started early is worth doing because it can add weeks, and the company we send it to can plan the location around it rather than after.

faqs.q: The bayou flooded. Is my air conditioning equipment damaged?
faqs.a: It depends how deep the water got in the crawlspace and how long it stayed. A unit that sat in an inch or two for a day will have damp insulation and corrosion starting at the base of the cabinet. A unit that was under water for days can have a seized motor, a flooded disconnect and damaged wiring. The first move is to get the system off so it does not run with water near the electrical, then dry the space out properly. Running a wet system can turn a water problem into a burned motor.

faqs.q: Why does my house have a crawlspace at all?
faqs.a: Because of the ground. In the low sections near the bayou, the water table sits close enough to the surface that a full height foundation would have been standing in wet soil much of the year. The builders raised the house on piers and left the space under it open and ventilated. That is a sensible answer to the flood problem, and it is also the reason the ductwork and the condensate drain sit where they sit, in the dampest, least visible part of the house.

faqs.q: My house is old but the air conditioning is newer. Why does it still struggle?
faqs.a: A newer condenser on an old house does not fix the house. If the duct system was built for a different layout, if the returns are undersized, or if the system was sized for a smaller version of the house, it will run long and still leave rooms warm. This is common where a 1950s house was extended and the system was replaced but the distribution was not. Checking the duct layout against the actual square footage tells you whether the problem is the machine or the path the air takes.

faqs.q: Is it worth moving my air handler out of the crawlspace?
faqs.a: It can be, and the deciding point is how often the space floods rather than how old the equipment is. A unit that gets wet every few years is a unit that gets replaced anyway, so the money spent moving it into the house is money spent once rather than money spent on a machine the bayou will take back. What drives the price of that work is how the new duct runs are routed, whether the floor has to be opened to connect them and how much of the original system can stay in place. We send the request to a company that already works Meyerland, and that company can look at the crawlspace and the house above it and tell you what could be reused.

faqs.q: Leaves and debris blow into the space under my house. Does that affect the cooling?
faqs.a: It does, and it is a condition of this canopy rather than of your house. The oak and elm cover along these streets is the densest in the city, and what falls off it drops through the crawlspace vents and collects on the floor of the space where the air handler and the duct trunk sit. That mat of leaf litter holds moisture against the cabinet and the trunk, and a duct lying on damp debris loses insulation and picks up a smell that moves into the supply air. Clearing the floor, keeping the vents screened and having the trunk checked for crushed or sagging sections are the three things that matter.
